content: 1. The etonogestrel and ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring is a contraceptive device that combines estrogen and progestin to prevent pregnancy. It is FDA-approved for this purpose. 2. The vaginal ring must be inserted into the vagina and left in place continuously for three weeks. After this period, it is removed for a one-week break, during which withdrawal bleeding typically occurs. A new ring is then inserted after the one-week interval. 3. The exact position of the vaginal ring within the vagina is not critical for its effectiveness. Users can choose a comfortable position for insertion, such as standing with one leg raised, squatting, or lying down. The ring should be compressed and inserted into the vagina. 4. If the ring is accidentally expelled and remains outside the vagina for less than three hours, contraceptive efficacy is not reduced. The ring can be rinsed with cool to lukewarm water and reinserted as soon as possible. 5. If the ring is out of the vagina for more than three continuous hours during the first or second week of use, contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. The ring should be reinserted immediately, and a barrier method, such as condoms with spermicide, must be used until the ring has been in place continuously for seven days. 6. During the third week, if the ring is expelled for more than three hours, it should be discarded, and one of two options should be followed: either insert a new ring immediately to start a new three-week cycle or wait up to seven days to insert a new ring, using a barrier method during this time. 7. If the ring-free interval exceeds one week, pregnancy should be ruled out, and a barrier method must be used until the new ring has been in place continuously for seven days. 8. The vaginal ring may interfere with the correct placement of a diaphragm, so diaphragms are not recommended as a backup method when using the ring. 9. The use of tampons does not affect the systemic absorption of hormones released by the vaginal ring. 10. The vaginal ring is contraindicated in women with a high risk of arterial or venous thrombosis, such as those who smoke and are over 35 years old, have a history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, or other thrombotic conditions. 11. Women with uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes with vascular disease, liver disease, or a history of breast cancer should not use the vaginal ring. It is also contraindicated in women with undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding or known hypersensitivity to its components. 12. The vaginal ring should not be used in women with a history of liver tumors or severe liver disease. If jaundice develops, the ring should be discontinued. 13. Women with a history of depression should be carefully monitored while using the vaginal ring, and its use should be discontinued if depression recurs to a serious degree. 14. The vaginal ring may increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and arterial thrombosis, such as stroke or myocardial infarction, particularly in women with additional risk factors like smoking, obesity, or a family history of VTE. 15. The risk of VTE is highest during the first year of combined hormonal contraceptive (CHC) use and after restarting CHCs following a break of at least four weeks. The risk gradually disappears after discontinuation of CHC use. 16. Women using the vaginal ring may experience unscheduled bleeding or spotting, especially during the first three months of use. If bleeding persists or occurs after previously regular cycles, pregnancy or malignancy should be ruled out. 17. The vaginal ring is not recommended for women with conditions that make the vagina more susceptible to irritation or ulceration. Vaginal or cervical erosion or ulceration has been reported in some users. 18. If a woman develops new, recurrent, persistent, or severe headaches while using the vaginal ring, the cause should be evaluated, and the ring should be discontinued if indicated. 19. Women with hypertriglyceridemia or a family history of this condition may be at increased risk of pancreatitis when using CHCs. 20. The vaginal ring is contraindicated in women who are currently pregnant or have confirmed pregnancy. If pregnancy is confirmed, the ring should be discontinued. 21. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who have used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy. There is also no evidence of teratogenic effects when CHCs are inadvertently used during early pregnancy. 22. Women with a history of CHC-related cholestasis or pregnancy-related cholestasis may be at increased risk for CHC-related cholestasis. 23. The vaginal ring may not be suitable for women with uncontrolled dyslipidemia, as some may experience adverse lipid changes while using CHCs. 24. If the vaginal ring is inadvertently inserted into the urinary bladder, it may require cystoscopic removal. Persistent urinary symptoms in users should prompt evaluation for this possibility. 25. Women who are breastfeeding should not use the vaginal ring until the child is weaned, as it may affect milk production and increase the risk of thromboembolism during the postpartum period. 26. The vaginal ring should not be used earlier than four weeks postpartum in women who are not breastfeeding, due to the increased risk of thromboembolism during the postpartum period. 27. Women with a history of migraines, especially those with aura or focal neurological symptoms, should use the vaginal ring with caution, as migraines may be prodromal of a cerebrovascular event. 28. The vaginal ring may increase the risk of gallbladder disease or worsen existing gallbladder conditions. Women with a history of CHC-related cholestasis or pregnancy-related cholestasis may be at increased risk. 29. If a woman misses two consecutive periods while adhering to the prescribed regimen, pregnancy should be ruled out. If the ring has been out of the vagina for more than three hours or the ring-free interval was extended beyond one week, pregnancy should also be considered. 30. Some women may experience amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea after discontinuing CHC use, particularly if these conditions were pre-existing.
